# The question we are answering

When psychologists publish a study, they recruit participants, and ideally they
tell the reader who those participants were: their gender, race, education, and
economic background. That information matters. If a study on memory or stress
only recruited young, white, college-educated participants but never says so, a
reader might wrongly assume the findings apply to everyone. The technical word
for this concern is representativeness.

This project asks two things. First, how often do psychology papers actually
report participant demographics? Second, has that reporting improved over time,
specifically from 2010 to 2026?

We focus on one journal, PLOS ONE, for three reasons: it is very large, it is
multidisciplinary, and it makes every article freely and openly available. That
openness is what lets us analyze tens of thousands of papers instead of a
handful.

Reading tens of thousands of papers by hand is not feasible, so the core idea is
to have a large language model (an AI system that can read and summarize text) go
through each paper's methods section and pull the demographic details into a
structured spreadsheet. We then analyze that spreadsheet for trends.

## The four time periods

To see change over time, we group the years into four stages that reflect
meaningful periods:

| Stage | Years | Rationale |
|-------|-------|-----------|
| Early | 2010 to 2014 | Baseline era |
| Middle | 2015 to 2019 | Settled, pre-pandemic |
| COVID | 2020 to 2023 | Pandemic disruption |
| Post-COVID | 2024 to 2026 | Recovery |

# What we extract from each paper

For every distinct group of participants a paper describes, we record whether,
and how, it reported each demographic. This coding scheme comes directly from the
project brief:

| Demographic | What we record |
|-------------|----------------|
| Gender | Reported? (yes/no) and the percentage breakdown (male / female / other) |
| Race | Reported? (yes/no) and the percentage breakdown (white / black / hispanic / asian / other) |
| Education | Reported? (yes/no) and the percentage with vs. without college |
| Socioeconomic status | A 0/1/2 scale: 0 = not reported, 1 = described only in words (e.g. "low income"), 2 = reported with an actual number (e.g. below $30,000) |

Two design details are worth calling out.

One row per participant group. A single paper might run three separate studies
with three different samples. Each becomes its own row in the spreadsheet, all
sharing the same article identifier (its DOI). This keeps the data honest, since
we do not average away real differences between a paper's samples.

Metadata for each article. Alongside the demographics, we record the publication
date, the corresponding author's institution, and the article's PLOS subject
tags.

## Which papers count

Not every article qualifies. An article is included only if it is an empirical
research article (not an editorial, correction, or review), published in PLOS
ONE, tagged by PLOS as psychology (any psychology subfield), and published
between 2010 and 2026. There is no minimum sample size, since the brief
explicitly wants all sample sizes.

# The pipeline as an assembly line

The whole system is a sequence of stages, each producing a file the next stage
consumes:

```
1. Find every qualifying psychology paper   ->  a master list (58,467 papers)   [DONE]
2. Draw a small pilot batch to test the AI  ->  46 papers                        [DONE]
3. Run the AI on the pilot                  ->  extracted demographics            [NEXT]
4. Grade the AI's accuracy by hand          ->  go / fix-and-retry decision
5. Run the AI on all 58,467 papers          ->  the full demographics table
6. Analyze the table                        ->  trends by year and stage (the answer)
```

We are currently at the end of stage 2. Stages 1 and 2 are done and verified.
Everything below documents how we got there and what remains.

## A note on infrastructure

All of this runs on Rivanna, the University of Virginia's high-performance
computing cluster. We use it for two reasons. The AI model is far too large to
run on a normal laptop, since it needs multiple high-end graphics cards. And the
full run over 58,467 papers is split into parallel chunks across many processors
so it finishes in a reasonable time. The code is written to survive
interruptions and reconnect cleanly, because these jobs run for hours and a
dropped connection should not lose work.

# Decision 1: where the data comes from

This was the most involved part of the project, and it is worth telling in full
because the twists shaped the final design. We started with one plan, hit four
separate problems, and ended up with a different and better architecture.

## The original plan: download everything

PLOS runs an open project called allofplos that lets you download every PLOS
article as a file. We did that: about 391,000 articles, roughly 9 GB compressed,
stored on the cluster. Each article file contains not just the text but PLOS's
own subject tags, which are arranged as a hierarchy:

```
Biology and life sciences  ->  Psychology  ->  Social psychology
```

The appeal was self-containment. Read those tags from each file, keep the ones
tagged psychology, and never touch the internet again. We wrote code to walk down
to the subfield sitting directly under "Psychology":

```python
def get_psychology_subfields(article):
    """Return the psychology subfield(s) an article is tagged with.
    e.g. Biology > Psychology > Social psychology  ->  ["Social psychology"]
    """
    subfields = []
    for node in article.subject_nodes:
        if node.text == "Psychology":
            # grab the tag(s) nested one level under Psychology
            subfields.extend(child.text for child in node.children)
    return subfields
```

## Detour A: the tag format had changed over the years

The first version found zero psychology papers, which was obviously wrong. To
find out why, we dumped the raw tag section of a few recent articles and looked
at it directly. The tags were there, but the container holding them had been
renamed. PLOS labels each block of tags with a type attribute. Older articles
used the type "Discipline"; newer articles used "Discipline-v3". Our code was
looking only for the exact word "Discipline", so it silently skipped every modern
article.

The fix was to accept any tag type that starts with "Discipline", which covers
both the old and new naming. After this change the psychology papers reappeared.
The lesson, which recurred later, is that PLOS's format is not constant across 15
years of articles, so assumptions about structure have to be checked against real
files rather than a single example.

## Detour B: "all subfields," not a fixed list

The brief named five subfields to study: social, cognitive, developmental,
clinical, and quantitative psychology. When we checked these against the real
data, two mismatches appeared. PLOS does not use the term "Quantitative
psychology" at all, so that category would have matched nothing. And PLOS does
use several subfields the brief never mentioned, including Experimental
psychology, Psychometrics, Behavior, and Emotions.

Rather than force the data into a preset list that did not fit it, we asked the
user how to proceed and they chose to include all subfields. So we switched to a
taxonomy-driven approach: keep every paper PLOS tags under Psychology, and record
whatever specific subfield PLOS assigned, whether or not it was on the original
list. This is more faithful to how the field actually organizes itself, and it
means the analysis can later group or filter by subfield however the researchers
want. In the final data this produced 23 distinct subfields rather than 5.

## Detour C: the 2015 mystery

With the tags parsing correctly, we ran the full scan over all 391,000 files and
produced a first master list. Before trusting it, we ran a basic sanity check:
count how many psychology papers we found in each year. The result contained an
alarming anomaly:

```
2014: 2,002 papers
2015:    12 papers    <- this cannot be right
2016: 2,100 papers
```

An almost empty year sitting between two full ones. A single-year hole is a
strong signal of a bug, not a real trend, so we investigated rather than
proceeding.

The first hypothesis was that publication dates were being read incorrectly for
2015, shunting those papers into the wrong year. We tested this by building a
histogram of every PLOS ONE article's year, regardless of subject. That showed
2015 was completely normal, with a healthy number of articles whose dates read as
2015. So dates were not the problem. The articles existed and were correctly
dated; they were simply not being recognized as psychology.

The second hypothesis was that the psychology detection was failing for 2015
specifically. We wrote a diagnostic that compared, per year, how many articles
our code tagged as psychology versus how many merely contained the string
"psycholog" anywhere in their tags:

```
year | total articles | tagged psychology | contains "psycholog"
2014 |      594       |        37         |         38
2015 |      561       |         1         |          1
2016 |      435       |        35         |         35
```

This was the key clue. For 2015, even the crude string search found almost
nothing, which meant the articles had essentially no subject tags at all, not
merely tags in an unexpected shape. To confirm, we printed the raw tag section of
several 2015 articles and tallied the tag-type attributes across the year. Almost
every 2015 article contained only this:

```xml
<article-categories>
  <subj-group subj-group-type="heading">
    <subject>Research Article</subject>
  </subj-group>
</article-categories>
```

That is a bare "Research Article" heading and nothing else. No discipline tags,
no psychology, no subject taxonomy of any kind. The tally confirmed it: of 561
sampled 2015 articles, 557 had no subject tags in their downloaded files.
Roughly 37% of 2013 articles had the same problem.

The diagnosis was therefore not a bug in our code but a gap in the data itself.
PLOS classified these papers on their website, but for that period they never
embedded the subject tags into the downloadable article files. You cannot read a
label that was never written into the file. Left unaddressed, this would have
erased almost all of 2015 and a large slice of 2013, gutting the Middle stage of
the analysis and any year-by-year trend through that period.

## The fix: use PLOS's search engine for discovery

The taxonomy is missing from the downloaded files, but it is not missing
everywhere. PLOS also runs a search engine, called Solr, that holds the
authoritative subject tags for every article, including the ones absent from the
files. So we changed strategy. Use the search engine to find which papers qualify
(discovery), and keep the downloaded files only for the one thing they reliably
contain, the full text the AI needs to read. This split, search engine for
discovery and downloaded files for full text, is in fact what the original
project brief proposed before we tried the download-only shortcut.

## Detour D: getting the search query right

Querying the search engine correctly took two lessons of its own, both found by
adding one filter at a time and watching the counts.

The first lesson: the search index contains far more than whole articles. It also
indexes fragments such as individual sections and figures. Without a specific
filter, doc_type:full, a query returns millions of these fragments instead of
articles. The second lesson: the constraints must be sent as strict filter
queries. A loosely written query is interpreted permissively by PLOS's endpoint
and effectively returns everything in the date range rather than only the
psychology papers.

With both lessons applied, we could watch each filter narrow the count in a way
that made sense:

```
q=*:* only                  : 3,487,529   (everything indexed, incl. fragments)
+ doc_type:full             :   411,419   (actual articles, all journals)
+ journal:"PLOS ONE"        :   332,150
+ article_type Research     :   313,425
+ date = 2015               :    28,107   (PLOS ONE research articles in 2015)
+ subject Psychology        :     4,346   (2015 psychology, recovered)
```

The relevant query, in plain form, is a set of filters combined together:

```python
filters = [
    'doc_type:full',                       # essential: whole articles only
    'journal:"PLOS ONE"',
    'article_type:"Research Article"',
    'subject:"Psychology"',
    f'publication_date:[{year}-01-01T00:00:00Z TO {year}-12-31T23:59:59Z]',
]
```

The year 2015 went from 12 papers under the file-only approach to 4,346 under the
search-engine approach. The search engine returns each subject as a full path,
such as /Biology and life sciences/Psychology/Cognitive psychology/Language, and
we read the subfield out of it the same way as before: the segment immediately
after "Psychology".

## Engineering detours worth recording

Two operational problems also came up while running on the cluster, and both are
the kind of thing that silently wastes time if undocumented.

The first was that batch jobs kept failing with a "module not found" error even
though the software was installed. The cause was that the standard command for
activating the software environment does not work the same way inside an
automated batch job as it does in an interactive terminal. It appeared to
succeed but left the job using the wrong Python. The fix was to point each job
directly at the correct Python interpreter by its full path, sidestepping the
activation step entirely.

The second was that a long-running data step, started in the background of a
terminal, died whenever the connection dropped. The cluster's web terminal tears
down background processes when the session ends. The fix was to submit that work
as a proper scheduled job instead, which runs independently of any terminal and
survives disconnects. Both fixes are now baked into the run scripts so they do
not have to be rediscovered.

## Data-quality issues we handled

Real-world data is messy, and the pipeline is built to tolerate two specific
kinds of imperfection.

One corrupted file. During the file scan, a single article file was truncated and
could not be read. The code logs it and moves on rather than crashing, since one
bad file out of 391,000 should not stop a multi-hour job.

Missing full text for recent papers. About 6% of the papers the search engine
found, mostly very recent 2025 and 2026 articles, are not yet in our downloaded
file snapshot, so we cannot read their full text. Those are flagged and set aside
so we never attempt to analyze a paper we cannot open.

# The finished master list

After switching to the search engine, the per-year counts are smooth, with no
gaps:

```python
total: 58,467 psychology articles
by year:
  2010:  853   2014: 4,249   2018: 3,492   2022: 3,761
  2011: 1,886  2015: 4,346   2019: 3,219   2023: 3,761
  2012: 2,481  2016: 3,663   2020: 3,548   2024: 4,249
  2013: 4,478  2017: 3,367   2021: 3,714   2025: 5,009
                                            2026: 2,391 (partial year)
by stage:
  early: 13,947   middle: 18,087   covid: 14,784   post-covid: 11,649
```

The year 2010 is genuinely smaller because PLOS ONE was a younger, smaller
journal then, which is a real trend rather than an error. The year 2026 is
partial because the year is not over.

# Decision 2: the pilot test batch

Before trusting the AI on 58,467 papers, we test it on a small batch and check
its work by hand. Two design choices matter here.

The sample is stratified, not purely random. If we picked papers purely at
random, common subfields like social and cognitive psychology would dominate and
rare ones might not appear at all. Instead we take two papers from each subfield,
so the test covers the full range of writing styles and topics.

The selection is reproducible. It uses a fixed random seed, so anyone re-running
it draws the exact same papers. That matters for a transparent, checkable
process.

```python
def stratified_sample(papers, per_subfield=2, seed=42):
    rng = random.Random(seed)                     # fixed seed = reproducible
    picked = []
    for subfield in all_subfields(papers):        # every subfield present
        candidates = [p for p in papers if subfield in p.subfields]
        if len(candidates) >= per_subfield:       # skip subfields with too few
            picked += rng.sample(candidates, per_subfield)
    return picked
```

Running it produced 46 papers across 23 subfields, including Social, Cognitive,
and Developmental psychology, Personality, Emotions, Psychometrics, and Behavior.
This is the batch the AI will be tested on.

# Decision 3: which AI model

The brief offered two candidate models, and we had to pick one:

| | Mistral-7B | Llama-3.3-70B (chosen) |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 7 billion parameters | 70 billion parameters |
| Accuracy on structured extraction | Weaker, more prone to missing or inventing numbers | Stronger, more reliable |
| Cost to run | Cheap, runs on modest hardware | Needs multiple high-end GPUs |

We chose Llama-3.3-70B. The deciding factor is accuracy, because a missed or
invented demographic percentage directly distorts the representativeness findings
that are the whole point of the study. Running on Rivanna removes the cost
concern that would otherwise favor the smaller model. The pilot exists precisely
to confirm this choice holds up before the full run.

# How the AI extraction works

Each paper's text is handed to the model with a precise instruction that spells
out exactly what to return and in what format:

```text
You are coding a psychology research article for a systematic review of
demographic reporting. For EACH distinct participant sample, extract:
 - gender: reported? (0/1) and percentage breakdown (male/female/other)
 - race:   reported? (0/1) and percentage breakdown (white/black/hispanic/asian/other)
 - education: reported? (0/1) and percentage with vs. without college
 - socioeconomic status: 0 = not reported, 1 = words only, 2 = a specific number

Respond with ONLY a JSON array, one element per sample, with these exact keys...
```

Two safeguards are built in. The output is format-checked, so the model must
return clean, structured data with exactly the required fields; anything
malformed is caught and flagged rather than silently polluting the dataset. And
the code pulls the paper's Methods and Participants text to the front before
handing it to the model, since that is where demographics almost always live,
which keeps the model focused on the relevant part of long papers.

# How the full run scales

Running 58,467 papers through a 70-billion-parameter model is heavy. The pipeline
handles this by splitting the work into independent chunks, called shards, that
run in parallel across many of the cluster's GPUs. Each chunk writes its own
results file, and the run is restartable: if a job is interrupted, it skips the
papers it already finished and picks up where it left off. That is essential for
jobs that run for hours and may be preempted.

# How the analysis answers the question

Once the full demographics table exists, the final step computes, for each
demographic and each year, and also for each of the four stages, two quantities.
The reporting rate is the fraction of samples that reported gender, race,
education, or socioeconomic status. The average composition is, for example, the
mean percentage female among papers that did report gender.

Plotting these across 2010 to 2026 is the direct answer to the original question:
whether demographic reporting in psychology is improving, and how it differs
across the early, middle, COVID, and post-COVID periods.

# Reproducibility: where everything lives

All code and documentation is version-controlled on GitHub (repository
SJ-Jain-systems/Halle). The project is organized so each stage is a separate,
testable piece:

```
src/
  solr_client.py          find psychology papers via PLOS's search engine
  build_index_solr.py     write the master list of 58,467 papers
  jats_xml.py             read metadata and full text from the article files
  sample_articles.py      draw the stratified pilot batch
  extract_demographics.py the AI instruction and strict format checking
  model_backend.py        run the Llama model on the GPUs
  run_pipeline.py         full run, split into restartable parallel chunks
  analyze_trends.py       compute reporting rates by year and stage
docs/
  DECISIONS.md            the three decisions, with full reasoning
  RUNNING_ON_RIVANNA.md   step-by-step run instructions for the cluster
  SCORING_RUBRIC.md       how we grade the AI's pilot accuracy
scripts/                  the diagnostics that caught the 2015 gap and more
tests/                    automated checks (33 of them) for the non-AI logic
```

Two points are worth emphasizing for anyone auditing this work. The logic is
tested: 33 automated tests cover the parsing, filtering, sampling, and analysis
code, that is everything except the AI itself, which is graded by hand on the
pilot. And the detours are documented rather than hidden: the diagnostic scripts
that uncovered the tag-format change and the 2015 gap are kept in the repository,
so the reasoning behind every design choice is traceable.
